items.title: Overlooked Blood Cell May Tracks Parkinson’s Brain Changes
items.snippet: Can blood platelets track Parkinson’s disease progression? Research from the Germans Trias i Pujol Research Institute (IGTP) demonstrates that platelets reflect neurodegenerative shifts—from mitochondrial breakdown to dementia onset—better than whole blood.

items.title: Premature Birth Alters Cerebellar Wiring
items.snippet: Why do premature infants face motor and language delays even without brain injuries? A landmark Science study led by Children's National reveals that developing outside the womb rewires the molecular programs of cerebellar Purkinje and granule cells, overturning the classic "catch-up" theory.

items.title: New Transporter Bypasses Blood-Brain Barrier to Deliver Creatine
items.snippet: How can drugs bypass the brain's tightest security checkpoint? Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland discovered that hijacking the sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter (SMVT) allows creatine derivatives to cross the blood-brain barrier, offering hope for rare deficiency syndromes.

items.title: Living Near Industrial Water Polluters Linked to Higher Risk of PSP
items.snippet: Can industrial water runoff trigger atypical parkinsonism? A 25-year study of 500,000 adults published in Neurology shows that living near facilities emitting pesticides, heavy metals, and organic pollutants is linked to a higher risk of progressive supranuclear palsy.

items.title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
items.snippet: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. items.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
items.snippet: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.
